name: Astarte
title: Canaanite and Phoenician goddess of fertility and war
summary: Astarte (Hebrew: Ashtoret, עשתרת) was a prominent Canaanite and Phoenician goddess associated with fertility, love, and war, with close parallels to the Mesopotamian Ishtar and the Sumerian Inanna. Throughout biblical history—from the time of the judges until just before the Babylonian exile—she represented one of the foremost rivals to Israel's God in the struggle for the people's loyalty. The Bible's authors portray the cult of Astarte as a fundamental violation of the first commandment and of the covenant relationship between the Lord and Israel. The book of Judges describes how the Israelites repeatedly turned to the goddesses of Astarte, while Solomon in his old age built high places for her worship. The prophets, from Samuel to Jeremiah, consistently condemned her worship and called the people back to faithfulness toward the one God. King Josiah's radical reform, in which he destroyed the shrines of Astarte, illustrates the biblical vision of a pure and undivided relationship with God.

keyEvents.title: The Israelites worship Astarte during the time of the judges
keyEvents.description: After Joshua's death, the people of Israel turned away from the Lord and began to worship Baal and the goddesses of Astarte, which aroused the Lord's anger and led him to hand them over to their enemies.

keyEvents.title: Samuel urges the people to turn back
keyEvents.description: The prophet Samuel asked the Israelites to remove the images of Astarte and foreign gods from among them and turn to the Lord alone. The people obeyed, and the Lord gave them victory over the Philistines.

keyEvents.title: The Philistines place Saul's armor in the temple of Astarte
keyEvents.description: After Saul fell in battle against the Philistines at Mount Gilboa, they took his armor and hung it up in the temple of Astarte in Beth-shan as a trophy to their goddess.

keyEvents.title: Solomon's idolatry
keyEvents.description: In his old age, King Solomon was led astray by his foreign wives to worship Astarte, the goddess of the Sidonians, and turned away from wholehearted loyalty to the Lord.

keyEvents.title: Josiah cleanses the land of Astarte worship
keyEvents.description: King Josiah carried out a thorough religious reform and destroyed the high places that Solomon had built for Astarte and other foreign gods on the hill east of Jerusalem, called the Mount of Corruption (part of the Mount of Olives).

keyEvents.title: Jeremiah warns against the Queen of Heaven
keyEvents.description: The prophet Jeremiah warned the people of Judah against offering sacrifices to "the Queen of Heaven," a figure likely linked to the cult of Astarte or Ishtar. The people refused to listen and insisted on continuing to offer incense and drink offerings to her.

versions.summary: Astarte (also called Ashtoreth) was a Canaanite and Phoenician goddess of fertility and war who was worshiped by the peoples surrounding Israel. She is mentioned repeatedly in the Bible as a symbol of idolatry that tempted the Israelites away from the Lord. The worship of Astarte was one of the most widespread forms of apostasy in Israel's history.

She was closely related to the Mesopotamian Ishtar and was worshiped throughout the ancient Middle East. In the Bible she is repeatedly mentioned as a symbol of the idolatry that tempted the Israelites away from the Lord. From the time of the judges through the monarchy, the cult of Astarte was one of the most widespread forms of religious apostasy in Israel and Judah, and the prophets consistently condemned her worship as a breach of the covenant with God.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew name 'Ashtoreth' (עשתרת) is likely a deliberate distortion of the original name, where the vowels from the Hebrew word 'boshet' (בושת, 'shame') were inserted to express contempt for the idol. The plural form 'Ashtaroth' (עשתרות) is also used in the Hebrew Bible and refers to the goddesses Astarte as a group.

Astarte was closely related to the Mesopotamian goddess Ishtar and the Sumerian Inanna. These goddesses shared functions linked to love, fertility, and war, and their worship spread throughout the ancient Near East. In Ugaritic texts (circa 1200 BCE), the goddess Athtart appears as a warrior deity closely associated with the god Baal.

Archaeologists have found a large number of small Astarte figurines in excavations across Israel and Judah, particularly from the Iron Age (circa 1200–586 BCE). These figurines, often called 'pillar figurines' (Judean Pillar Figurines), depict a woman with prominent breasts and were likely connected to fertility rituals or protective practices in homes. Over a thousand such figurines have been found in Jerusalem alone.

The identification of the 'queen of heaven' (מלכת השמים) in the book of Jeremiah with Astarte is debated among scholars. Some argue it refers to the Mesopotamian Ishtar, while others see it as a syncretic figure combining traits from several goddesses. The cult included baking cakes shaped like the goddess, offering incense, and pouring drink offerings.

Astarte's temple in Beth-Shean, where the Philistines hung up Saul's armor according to 1 Samuel 31:10, has been confirmed through archaeological excavations. The digs have revealed several temple structures from the late Bronze Age and early Iron Age, and the city had a long history of Canaanite and Egyptian cultic practices.

In rabbinic tradition, Astarte worship was viewed as one of the most serious forms of idolatry. The Talmud (Sanhedrin 63b) discusses how the Israelites were drawn to foreign cults and links this to the evil inclination (yetzer hara). Maimonides later classified all Astarte worship under the prohibition against idolatry in his legal codifications.

Phoenician inscriptions from Sidon (circa 500 BCE) mention Astarte as the city's chief goddess and associate her with the Sidonian royal house. This sheds light on the biblical connection between Astarte and the Sidonians, who are mentioned in relation to Solomon's apostasy.

The place name Ashtaroth-Karnaim ('Astarte of the two horns'), mentioned in Genesis 14:5, testifies that Astarte worship was widespread in Transjordan already in the patriarchal period. Horns were a common symbol of divine power in the ancient Near East, and Astarte was often depicted with crescent-shaped horns.
